definition: Modeling a completely new, hand-sculpted mesh for a VFX element — the source's own example is a dust cloud at a character's feet — for every single frame it appears in, rather than using a particle system or one continuously-deforming mesh, so the effect's own shape changes in the same sharp, discrete, hand-authored steps as the stepped-keyed character it accompanies.
purpose: Keep an effect visually consistent with a stepped, hand-posed character performance, where a standard particle system's smooth, physically-simulated behavior would look conspicuously 'more 3D' than the character next to it.
visible_effect: An effect's silhouette changes in sharp, distinct, deliberately-sculpted steps frame to frame, rather than evolving continuously the way a particle system or a single deforming mesh would.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Preserves the production's own stated all-encompassing edict ('kill everything 3D... everything on screen had to be an intentional and artistic choice, not a computer's automated solution') for EFFECTS specifically, not just characters — a particle system is, by this source's own framing, exactly the kind of 'computer's automated solution' the studio was trying to eliminate everywhere.
physical_interpretation: None — explicitly not a simulation of any physical dust/smoke behavior; a hand-sculpted substitute for one.
use_cases: a small number of effect instances on screen at once (this source's own context: a competitive fighting game with at most two characters rendered), where the per-frame authoring cost is affordable specifically because of that low instance count
an effect placed close to, or interacting directly with, a stepped-keyed character, where a smoothly-simulated effect would visually clash with the character's own discrete posing
non_use_cases: any effect that needs to be reused cheaply across many characters, contexts, or simultaneous instances — a particle system's entire value proposition (reuse, parameterization, low per-instance cost) is given up completely
an effect whose motion needs to react procedurally to live gameplay state rather than playing back a fixed, pre-authored sequence
any production without the specific art-budget headroom this source's own reaction ('and that is bonkers') frames as an extreme, not a default, choice even within a AAA-adjacent production
interactions: stepped_keyframes_replace_interpolation_for_2d_read and per_key_pose_imperfection_defeats_rigid_3d_read (video 51, this batch) — the same 'hand-posed, deliberately imperfect, not a computer's automated result' principle applied to VFX GEOMETRY rather than character rig bones

motion_smear_readability (W01) — a much cheaper alternative technique for fast-motion readability; this same batch's video 52 also separately notes the two games in this comparison chose different alternatives (smears vs. old-school speed lines) for that different, cheaper problem, which this entry's technique is not solving

style_variations.anime: an extreme, high-budget-only technique even within this style, per the source's own framing
style_variations.realistic: no equivalent — realistic VFX defaults to continuous simulation specifically because that IS the goal

cadence_representation: Not represented, and not a close fit for either of this build's two VFX paths. `ai/vfxspec.js` targets the `kind:'vfx'` emitter item as a declarative, parametric, reversible effect — closer to a particle system than to hand-sculpted per-frame geometry. `pnx/**`'s procedural node graph describes effects through fields and nodes, not as a sequence of discretely-authored meshes either. A literal 'different hand-sculpted mesh every frame' sequence is closer to a raw keyframed-geometry animation than to anything either existing VFX system currently expresses, and neither is a natural extension for it — this is recorded as real, well-evidenced production knowledge with a clear capability gap rather than forced onto either path.
control_surface: None currently reaches this in either VFX system.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Not measurable in this build: no track type stores raw per-frame mesh geometry as a keyed asset, in the character rig system or in either VFX system.
failure_modes: cost scaling directly with frame count AND instance count, with zero reuse across characters or contexts — the source's own 'and that is bonkers' reaction is itself evidence this is recognized internally as an extreme choice, not a default one
applying it to an effect that later needs to scale to many simultaneous instances or respond to live/reactive gameplay state, neither of which this technique supports at all
roblox_considerations: Roblox's native effect tooling (`ParticleEmitter`, `Beam`) is built around continuous/parametric behavior, much closer to what `ai/vfxspec.js` already targets than to this technique. A literal frame-swapped `MeshPart`/`SpecialMesh` sequence is possible in Roblox (swapping `MeshId` per frame) but would be exactly as extreme a departure from Roblox's own normal effect-authoring idioms as it was from this source's own general-purpose 3D engine.
performance_implications: Significant per-instance modeling/authoring cost, explicitly called out by the source as unusual; no distinct RUNTIME cost claim is made, since rendering a swapped mesh costs the same as rendering any other mesh.
examples: 'when necessary for certain effects like the clouds of dust at a character's feet, they modeled those clouds in 3d frame by frame, and that is bonkers' (video @ 11:54–12:14)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/kZsboyfs-L4 @ 11:54–12:14 — Dan (New Frame Plus) states the technique directly, sourced from the same studio's own GDC talk this video cites throughout; transcript-only, no frames extracted this session; experimental until validated
